questions.knowledge_point: Partial Derivatives as Limits of Difference Quotients
questions.worked_solution:
The derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is given by the limit 

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{f(x,y+h)-f(x,y)}{h}).
$$

Since $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{(y+2)^{3}},$  we have that 

$$
f(x,y+h)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{(y+h+2)^{3}}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}={lim}_{h\to 0}[\frac{1}{h}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{(y+h+2)^{3}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{(y+2)^{3}})].
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Partial Derivatives of Two-Variable Functions
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy+{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy)+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡y) \\  & =x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y)+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) \\  & =x\cdot 1+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =x+\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

The notation ${f}_{y}$ denotes the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y.$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the sum rule for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{2x+3y}+{x}^{2}{y}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{2x}\cdot {e}^{3y})+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{y}^{3}) \\  & ={e}^{2x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{3y})+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{3}) \\  & ={e}^{2x}\cdot 3{e}^{3y}+{x}^{2}\cdot 3{y}^{2} \\  & =3{e}^{2x+3y}+3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Partial Derivative at a Point
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants:

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-xy) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y)-\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡y\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-y\cdot (1) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡x-y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(0,\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,\pi ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡0-\pi  \\  & =(-1)\cdot 1-\pi  \\  & =-\pi -1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Partial Derivative at a Point
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants:

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{sec}⁡y+{x}^{4}y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{sec}⁡y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{4}y) \\  & =x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sec}⁡y)+{x}^{4}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y) \\  & =x\cdot (\operatorname{sec}⁡y\operatorname{tan}⁡y)+{x}^{4}\cdot (1) \\  & =x\operatorname{sec}⁡y\operatorname{tan}⁡y+{x}^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(\sqrt{2},\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(\sqrt{2},\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+{(\sqrt{2})}^{4} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot 1+4 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y)=4y{x}^{2}-x{y}^{4},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ at the point $(2,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants:

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4y{x}^{2}-x{y}^{4}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4y{x}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{4}) \\  & =4{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y)-x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{4}) \\  & =4{x}^{2}\cdot (1)-x\cdot (4{y}^{3}) \\  & =4{x}^{2}-4x{y}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y}{|}_{(2,1)} & =4\cdot {2}^{2}-4\cdot 2\cdot {1}^{3} \\  & =16-8 \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y)={x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡y-2y\sqrt{x},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ at the point $(1,e).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants:

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡y-2y\sqrt{x}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡y)-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y\sqrt{x}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3})-2y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{x}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡y\cdot (3{x}^{2})-2y\cdot (\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}) \\  & =3{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡y-\frac{y}{\sqrt{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(1,e)} & =3\cdot {1}^{2}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡e-\frac{e}{\sqrt{1}} \\  & =3-e\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡y+{x}^{7}y,$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ at the point $(1,\frac{1}{2}).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants:

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡y+{x}^{7}y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{7}y) \\  & ={e}^{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)+{x}^{7}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y) \\  & ={e}^{x}\cdot (\frac{1}{y})+{x}^{7}\cdot (1) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x}}{y}+{x}^{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,\frac{1}{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y}{|}_{(1,1/2)} & =\frac{{e}^{1}}{(\frac{1}{2})}+{1}^{7} \\  & =2e+1\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Partial Derivatives as Limits of Difference Quotients
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $f(x,y) = y^2\ln{x},$ express $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ as the limit of a difference quotient.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ is given by the limit 

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \lim_{h \to 0} \left(\dfrac{f(x+h,y)-f(x,y)}{h}\right).
$$

Since $f(x) = y^2 \ln{x},$  we have that 

$$
f(x+h,y) = y^2\ln(x+h).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\displaystyle \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \lim_{h \to 0}\left( \dfrac{y^2\ln(x+h) -y^2\ln{x} }{h}\right).
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding Partial Derivatives of Two-Variable Functions
canonical_examples.problem: Find $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ given that $f(x,y) = 3x\ln y + 2ye^x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+2y{e}^{x}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x\operatorname{ln}⁡y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y{e}^{x}) \\  & =3x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)+2{e}^{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y) \\  & =3x\cdot \frac{1}{y}+2{e}^{x}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{3x}{y}+2{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Partial Derivative at a Point
canonical_examples.problem: For the function $f(x,y) = x^2y^2+\sin{x}\cos{y},$ evaluate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ at the point $(\pi,2\pi).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants:

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & ={y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & ={y}^{2}\cdot (2x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡y\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =2x{y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(\pi,2\pi)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(\pi ,2\pi )} & =2\cdot \pi \cdot (2\pi )^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi  \\  & =2\pi \cdot 4{\pi }^{2}+(-1)\cdot 1 \\  & =8{\pi }^{3}-1\end{aligned}
$$
